chunks.text: The peepal, or sacred fig, is a large, long-lived fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent and parts of mainland Southeast Asia, capable of reaching about 30 metres with heart-shaped leaves drawn out into a long drip-tip and small green figs that ripen to purple. Botanically it depends entirely on a single species of fig wasp for pollination, a relationship so specific that the wasp lays its eggs only in this tree's flowers, and the tree in turn can become a problematic coloniser outside its native range, since it often germinates as an epiphyte high in the crown of a host tree and sends roots down to strangle it over time. Its religious weight, however, is what sets it apart: it is sacred to four religions that trace their origins to the Indian subcontinent — Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism. In Hindu tradition it is the ashwattha of the Rigveda and the Bhagavad Gita, associated with the Trimurti, circumambulated seven times by devotees chanting salutations to the 'king of trees', and meditated beneath by wandering ascetics. Its single most famous individual role is in Buddhism: Siddhartha Gautama is said to have attained enlightenment seated beneath a tree of this species at Bodh Gaya, in present-day Bihar, and while the original tree has been destroyed and replanted more than once over the centuries, a descendant planted around 288 BCE at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, is documented as the oldest living tree of known planting date anywhere in the world, well over 2,250 years old. Peepal-leaf motifs appear on seals from the Indus Valley Civilisation more than four thousand years ago, its outline was later adopted as the design basis for India's Bharat Ratna civilian honour, and it is the official state tree of Odisha, Bihar and Haryana today. Traditional medicine across the subcontinent also credits various parts of the tree with uses against roughly fifty different ailments, from asthma to diabetes, though these are traditional rather than clinically established claims.
